title: Nick McConnell - Things I've Learnt from Maintaining Angband
speaker: Nick McConnell
talk_title: Things I've Learnt from Maintaining Angband
description: I'll give a personal view of what it's been like doing Angband and variant development, especially being actual Angband maintainer. I'm likely to include things like why I got into it in the first place, how Angband has progressed over the years, and what people expect from Angband and its maintainers. I want to leave plenty of time for Q&A.

chapters.title: Everyone has a different view of Angband
Games and their traditions influence each other
Making a variant frees you from history
Having a vision is good, but so is listening
Best practice is getting stuff done

segments.text: I am pleased to introduce Nick McConnell.
Welcome, Nick.
Nick: Hey.
EMCEE: You are currently involved in egg man and have been since 2005.
That's a long time.
Take it away and talk about with an it is like working on Angband.
Nick: Before starting, big thanks to the organizers and being friendly and making everything work
well.
Also, a huge thanks to all the previous speakers.
There have been a truly excellent array of talks and my mind is in shreds from continually
being blown by all of them.
We will see how I go with keeping a coherent narrative here.
I have always wanted to go to the Roguelike Celebration and being in Australia that is
difficult.
Given it is online this year, this has been a good opportunity and happily the organizers
approached me, or rather approached the current Angband team, to see if I would be able to
give a talk.
I thought great.
I will do that.
I had no idea what I was going totalk -- to talk about it.
I didn't know what people would be interested in about Angband.
I thought I will run through a few quick things and leave a lot of time for people to ask
questions about what they are actually interested.
That's the game plan and hopefully I will say some interest things along the way but
we will see.
For those who don't know, Angband descendent of UMoria and it is -- I am a long way from
being an industry professional.
It is a free open source game written entirely in large quantities of C and operated on by
volunteers in their spare time basically.
Thing number one and here is where I will talk about a little history.
Angband was developed from Umoria in 1999 by some students in the UK.
It floated around the university for a few years and then in 1993 it was released on
to the then fairly embryonic internet.
And then, you know, in those days, things, code was often not very portable so then there
was a port to the PC and the MAC and things like this.
And time went on and the internet gradually improved and somewhere around about the mid-90s
Angband had a moment where a lot of people were getting to play it.
It was a theme in the Zeitgeist of the internet at the time.
But the other thing about it is that since it started in 1990 it has been in continuous
development for that entire time.
It's a very interesting thing to observe because I will put out a new version, occasionally,
and some of the comments that you get on that are Angband, why would you change that?
I mean, it was good already, wasn't it?
And you don't know where to start with a comment like that because um, first, I am hoping that
my new version is making it better, and also, I don't know which bit you are talking about
was already good.
Do you know 2.6?
What?
I don't know.
A game that has existed over such a long span has a very eclectic range of viewpoints that
people have of it.
But, you know, it is still a great thing to be maintainer of.
OK.
Second point and again, this is kind of a function of being a really long-term game.
Traditions build up over how to play games.
People play the game, they talk about it, the developers listen to what the people who
are playing are talking about, they fix bugs, they incorporate new features that people
think might be interesting, and so you have this symbiosis between the game and its tradition.
Angband had a particular twist on that because it was extensively modelled in the '90s particularly
so there was a huge array of Angband variants so you had this constant process of people
writing their on mod for Angband, releasing it as a variant, the original maintainers
then absorbing bits of that back into the main game.
And so you get this long, interweaving process of the game and the tradition.
And there is another very interesting thing that happened with Angband specifically here
where it was assumed for a very long time that the best way to play Angband was extraordinarily
conservatively.
It is a big, long game.
You have to dive to the bottom of a 100 level dungeon and kill the main boss.
It is very easy to die along the way obviously.
It was accepted wisdom that you would play slowly and carefully because you really didn't
want to die so it made it a very long game and that made people even more conservative
because you wouldn't want to loose a month's worth of play because you did something careless
or played tired or your Cat stood on the keyboard.
So this was believed for a long time.
Conservative play.
You have got to do it.
Don't go below level 20 without having free action that sort of thing.
Somewhere in the mid-2000s, some players starting saying no, that's not the best way to play.
It is not just boring but you are actually better in terms of number of games you complete
successfully to play aggressively, to dive hard, to take down stairs as soon as you can,
and to, you know, sure you will lose some characters but you can play five characters
to level 20 in the same time as you used to be playing one to level 24.
And so, this is an interesting example, I think, of when the tradition has actually
changed gameplay considerably and that has in turn influenced the development rather
than the assumption being everybody will be being ultraconservative the assumption now
is people are probably not being ultraconservative.
Although Angband is a game which fundamentally doesn't tell its players how to play it so
there will still be some doing conservative play as well presumably.
Now, Angband does have a long tradition and on a good day that's a wonderful thing.
It is, you know, a maintainer of a game that been around for a long time.
It has a proud history and in Roguelike games and games in general.
On a bad day that's all just baggage.
One thing that you can do which frees you from this baggage is to just fork the game.
Make a new variant.
You know, it can be themed around something, it can just have some tweaks you like, wharf
-- whatever.
Typically the community as a whole is very accepting of this.
They will be quite hard on the original game and complain about things that go wrong but
if somebody puts out a variant they will be excited about it and positive and say yes,
you know, there are wonderful ideas in this game and by the way, you should know every
time you read a scroll the game crashes but they are still very accepting.
This is, you know, people talk a lot about having a vision for a game and certainly as
a game developer, you have to have a vision, and you have to have an idea of what you should
be doing.
And you have grand plans but very commonly, you put your grand plans into effect, and
you put out the game, and some people will not like what you are done and sometimes a
lot of people won't like what you have done.
It is very good to get feedback, early feedback if possible, something suggested yesterday
was one of the things most useful to do is do early play testing and putting it out to
the players early is a very good way to get early feedback and something I would advise
for everybody.
Best practice is getting stuff done.
Yeah.
So the whole plate early thing is a good idea.
Also, if you want to make progress on improving your game, particularly if it is an existing
game that is out there, avoiding going down rabbit holes is a really good idea, actually,
it is probably even more true if it is not an existing game out there and you are still
developing it.
I mean, you want to do it right and you want to do it well but sometimes you just need
to do to and get it out there.
Final one, and hopefully leaving a little time for questions, community.
The Angband community is just awesome.
We have forums we talk on, we discuss improvements to the game, we discuss what is right with
it, we discuss what is wrong with it.
And so many ideas that I have had or that other people have had have been improved massively
by discussion and by play testing and so on.
And the Roguelike community I have particularly discovered over the last two days is absolutely
great.
You people are all part of that.
Give yourselves a pat on the back.
You are awesome.
And now chance for questions.
EMCEE: Excellent.
I would agree the two days has been a showcase of a lot of the lovely people in the community.
And yeah, we do have plenty of questions.
More than we will have time to get into unfortunately.
But we will go through a couple.
Starting with Evan who asked what do you add or change in a game that's been around for
a decade?
>> Oh, lots of things.
It can get a little oslified and you can get mechanics that no longer work the way they
intended to.
You look at traps.
Traps became a thing where the general idea is simple.
You are walk along, hit a trap, something bad happens.
You had to work out ways for the player getting around that.
They had to have perception to notice the trap or spells to detect traps and it degenerated
to the point where every character would get easy trap detection early on in the game.
Now, what's the point?
Everybody just detects the traps and you know, it is a press button not to die sort of scenario.
A few years back, we completely reworked the trap system so that traps were interesting
again.
And there are a whole lot of mechanics like that where maybe it started off in a, you
know, in a way that worked and it has gradually degenerated over time or where it never really
worked but nobody was saying anything.
EMCEE: Right.
A chance to deossify and shake off the calcium.
I think we have one more question.
Has egg man changed due to speed runner interest?
Is that something that's come up?
>> Not a huge amount.
It has always been -- there have been competitions.
There is an ongoing Angband competition thing and that is usually judged by Turn Count so
speed running has always been a kind of a thing to some extent.
It is probably not a new thing for Angband.
EMCEE: Right.
It has just been a part of it for the history of it.
Cool.
All right.
